To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the identifiability issue in ICA is not solved by simply assuming that the data is generated by independent components; (ii) the identifiablity issue is solved by assuming that the mixing process is governed by independent mechanisms; (iii) this approach can be used to solve problems that have not been solvable by ICA before.

(1) independent component analysis (ICA) is non-identifiable for nonlinear mixing, and (2) the identifiability can be restored by including assumptions reflecting the causal principle of independent mechanisms.

(a) we introduce a new approach to nonlinear blind source separation, (b) the new approach has better performance than previous methods, and (c) the new approach can be applied to a wider class of problems than previous approaches.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
a novel perspective on unsupervised learning, where we consider the latent code as a causal mechanism that influences the mixing process.
a novel approach to unsupervised representation and dimensionality reduction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ICA is not the only solution to blind source separation, but that there are many other approaches, and that some of them can be justified in terms of causal assumptions.
ICA is not a good model for the data generating process, and that the ICA model is not a useful tool for the analysis of the data generating process.
the proposed approach is not a new concept, but a new application of a well-known concept.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show how to use causal assumptions in a principled way to improve the identifiability in blind source separation.
we propose a new approach to blind source separation which is able to deal with nonlinear mixing.
we have shown that the principle of independent mechanism analysis can be used to identify latent variables from nonlinear mixtures of them, even when the mixing process is unknown.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the presence of nonlinear mixtures, the principle of independent mechanisms can provide a useful alternative to statistical independence as a basis for representation learning.
independent mechanism analysis can provide a principled framework in which to study the identifiability problem in nonlinear blind source recovery.
the principle of independent mechanism is a viable alternative to the principle of independent source for unsupervised learning of latent codes.
